alabama.agency_name: Alabama Department of Public Health, Center for Health Statistics (Vital Records)
alabama.birth_certificate: Apply to the Alabama Department of Public Health, Center for Health Statistics (Vital Records), using the Application to Change an Alabama Birth or Death Certificate (form ADPH-HS-33). Under Ala. Code § 22-9A-19(d), you must submit a certified copy of a court order stating that your sex has been changed by surgical procedure (and reflecting any name change). The fee to amend a birth certificate is $20, which includes one certified copy; additional copies are $6 each, and expedited processing adds $15.
alabama.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required to change the sex on a birth certificate, while a driver's license can instead be changed with a surgeon's letter alone.
alabama.drivers_license: Apply in person at an Alabama Law Enforcement Agency (ALEA) driver license office under ALEA Policy Order 63. You must present either an amended birth certificate or a letter on the surgeon's letterhead stating you have had complete and irreversible sex reassignment surgery. The Eleventh Circuit upheld this policy in Corbitt v. Taylor on September 20, 2024. No X marker is available; only M or F.
alabama.marker_overview: Alabama is restrictive: changing the gender marker requires proof of surgery, and a birth-certificate change also requires a court order. A driver's license can be changed with an amended birth certificate or a surgeon's letter. Alabama offers only M or F markers — there is no X nonbinary option.
alabama.surgery_required: Yes — Alabama requires proof of sex-change surgery for both a birth-certificate change (via the court order) and a driver's license change (via the surgeon's letter or an amended birth certificate).

alaska.agency_name: Alaska Department of Health, Health Analytics and Vital Records
alaska.birth_certificate: Apply to the Alaska Department of Health, Health Analytics and Vital Records (Special Services Unit), with the Alaska Birth Certificate Request Form, a photocopy of your ID, and either a letter from a physician, social worker, psychologist, professional counselor, physician assistant, or advanced nurse practitioner, or a certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex. The ACLU of Alaska lists a $60 fee for the amendment and one certified copy; confirm the current fee with Vital Records before submitting.
alaska.court_order_required: No — a court order is not required for either document; it is simply one accepted alternative to the professional certification.
alaska.drivers_license: Apply in person at an Alaska Division of Motor Vehicles office with a D1 application and Form 427, Certification for Change of Sex Designator. Form 427 must be completed and certified by a physician, social worker, psychologist, professional counselor, physician assistant, or advanced nurse practitioner — unless you instead present an amended birth certificate, a valid U.S. passport, or a court order granting a change of sex or gender. No X marker is available; only M or F.
alaska.marker_overview: Alaska allows gender-marker changes on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID with certification from a medical or other qualified professional — no court order and no surgery are required. The state does not offer an X nonbinary marker on either document.
alaska.surgery_required: No — Alaska does not require surgery; the professional certification states only that you have had appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition.

arizona.agency_name: Arizona Department of Health Services, Bureau of Vital Records
arizona.birth_certificate: Apply to the Arizona Department of Health Services, Bureau of Vital Records. There are two routes: (1) the direct route under A.R.S. § 36-337(A)(3), with a written request, a birth-certificate request form, an affidavit to correct the record, and a notarized physician statement verifying a sex-change operation or a chromosomal count establishing a different sex; or (2) the court-order route under § 36-337(A)(4), by obtaining a court order directing ADHS to amend the record. The Ninth Circuit held on October 6, 2026, in Roe v. Johnston, that the court-order route is available without proof of specific medical treatments, after a district court had struck the surgery requirement in September 2025. No fee was stated in the sources checked — confirm the current fee with ADHS before submitting.
arizona.court_order_required: No — a court order is not required for a driver's license, and for a birth certificate it is one of two routes: the route that avoids any surgery requirement.
arizona.drivers_license: Apply in person at a full-service Arizona Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Division office with a signed physician letter on official letterhead, including the physician's license number and dated within three months, stating you are irrevocably committed to the gender-change process and have received appropriate clinical treatment. A certified court order is needed only if you are also changing your name. The replacement license fee is $12. No X marker is published on an official ADOT page, so confirm X availability with MVD before relying on it.
arizona.marker_overview: Arizona allows gender-marker changes, but the birth-certificate rules shifted in 2025–2026 through litigation: the direct vital-records route still requires proof of surgery, while a court-order route now requires no specific medical treatment. A driver's license can be changed with a physician's letter, with no court order needed.
arizona.surgery_required: No — no surgery is required if you use the court-order route for a birth certificate or the physician-letter route for a license, but the direct ADHS birth-certificate route under § 36-337(A)(3) does require proof of a sex-change operation.

arkansas.agency_name: Arkansas Department of Health, Vital Records
arkansas.birth_certificate: Apply to the Arkansas Department of Health, Vital Records, by submitting a certified court order specifying the name change and stating that the sex is to be changed due to a surgical procedure, as required by Ark. Code § 20-18-307(d). The Department states that an attorney is normally needed to obtain this type of court order. The Department lists a $15 amendment fee, and a certified copy of a birth certificate is $12 for the first copy and $10 for each additional copy ordered at the same time.
arkansas.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for the birth-certificate change, and because a driver's license change requires an amended birth certificate, a court order is effectively required for both.
arkansas.drivers_license: Apply to the Department of Finance and Administration, Office of Driver Services, using its form and submitting an original or certified copy of an amended birth certificate — either from Arkansas under § 20-18-307 or from another state's vital records office — under 27 CAR § 34-104. Act 711 of 2025 (HB 1796) requires licenses and IDs to show M for male or F for female only; the state will not issue a license or ID showing X or with no gender information.
arkansas.marker_overview: Arkansas is restrictive: a birth-certificate change requires a court order stating the person's sex was changed by surgical procedure, and a driver's license change now requires an amended birth certificate. Act 711 of 2025 codified that licenses and IDs show M or F only, with no X marker.
arkansas.surgery_required: Yes — the birth-certificate amendment requires a court order stating that sex was changed by surgical procedure, and the license change depends on that amended birth certificate.

california.agency_name: California Department of Public Health, Vital Records
california.birth_certificate: Apply to the California Department of Public Health, Vital Records, using form VS 24B, Application to Amend a Birth Record, with a sworn statement under penalty of perjury that the change conforms to your gender identity and is not made for any fraudulent purpose. No court order or medical documentation is required. The fee for changing the sex field is $26, including one copy of the new record, with additional certified copies at $31 each.
california.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed for either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order (form NC-300) is optional and mainly useful if you are also changing your legal name or need an order for use in another state.
california.drivers_license: Apply at the California Department of Motor Vehicles by completing a new driver license or ID application and selecting male, female, or nonbinary (X) as your gender category; the DMV cannot require any documentation beyond your own self-certification. You must visit a DMV office in person to finalize the change. The fee for a Class C driver's license is $37.
california.marker_overview: California allows gender-marker changes on a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with no court order, medical documentation, or surgery required. You may choose male, female, or nonbinary (X) on state documents under the Gender Recognition Act (SB 179).
california.surgery_required: No — California requires no surgery, medical treatment, or doctor's letter for a gender-marker change on either document.

colorado.agency_name: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, Vital Records
colorado.birth_certificate: Apply to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, Vital Records, with a written request signed under penalty of law and a self-statement, also signed under penalty of law, confirming that the sex designation on the birth certificate does not align with your gender identity, under C.R.S. § 25-2-113.8. The state issues a new birth certificate showing M, F, or X that is not marked as amended. A provider statement is required only for minors. The one-time limit on self-requested birth-certificate changes was repealed in 2025 (HB 25-1312), but confirm with CDPHE if you need a further change, as its published materials still describe further changes as requiring a court order.
colorado.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed for an adult's first changes; a court order is required only for further changes after the self-requested limits (after three DMV changes since October 1, 2026, or a further birth-certificate change).
colorado.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Colorado Division of Motor Vehicles driver license office with form DR 2083, Change of Sex Designation, signed under penalty of law, or with a new Colorado birth certificate. Adults self-attest and may choose M, F, or X; there is no additional fee beyond the standard fee for a new credential. Applicants under 18 need a health care provider and a parent, guardian, or legal representative to sign the form. Since October 1, 2026, a sex designation may be changed on request up to three times; any further change requires a certified court order.
colorado.marker_overview: Colorado allows gender-marker changes on a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation for adults, with no court order, doctor's letter, or surgery required. M, F, and X markers are available on both documents under Jude's Law.
colorado.surgery_required: No — Colorado law expressly does not require any specific surgery, treatment, clinical care, or behavioral health care to update a sex designation.

connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Records
connecticut.birth_certificate: Apply to the Connecticut Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Records, by mailing a notarized affidavit from you (signed under penalty of law) requesting a replacement birth certificate, a notarized affidavit from a licensed physician, physician assistant, advanced practice registered nurse, or psychologist stating you have undergone surgical, hormonal, or other treatment clinically appropriate for gender transition, and a photocopy of a valid government-issued photo ID. A certified copy of a court order is needed only if you are also changing your name. A certified copy costs $30.
connecticut.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is required only if you are also changing your legal name.
connecticut.drivers_license: Apply at the Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles by surrendering your current license or ID, submitting the completed Gender Designation form (B-385) selecting Female (F), Male (M), or Non-Binary (X), and paying the applicable fee for a new or updated credential, with a new photograph taken. DMV staff must not request additional gender-related information beyond the form. A parent or guardian must sign for a minor, or the minor must submit a signed and notarized parental-consent form.
connecticut.marker_overview: Connecticut allows gender-marker changes on a birth certificate with affidavits from you and a health care provider, and on a driver's license or state ID by self-selection on a DMV form, with no court order and no surgery required. Female, male, and nonbinary (X) markers are available.
connecticut.surgery_required: No — surgery is not required; the provider affidavit may instead state that you have had hormonal or other treatment clinically appropriate for gender transition, and the surgical requirement was removed in 2015.

delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Health and Social Services, Office of Vital Statistics
delaware.birth_certificate: Apply to the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services, Office of Vital Statistics, with a birth certificate application, a Requester's Affidavit for Sex Change on Birth Certificate, a Healthcare Provider's Affidavit for Sex Change on Birth Certificate from a medical or mental health professional stating you have had surgical, hormonal, psychological, or other treatment appropriate for you for gender transition, a valid photo ID, and your original birth certificate (or a $25 fee if you no longer have the original). Include a certified copy of a name-change order only if you are also changing your name. The X marker is not available on a birth certificate under the current rules.
delaware.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either document; a court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name.
delaware.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles office with Form MV2020, Request for Gender Change on Driver License/Identification Card. Section C must be completed by a medical or social service provider licensed in the United States certifying that your gender is male or female; surgery is not required, and the form cannot be processed by mail or online. A separate applicant-signed Gender Designation Change Consent Form is reported to allow an X marker, but the National Center for Transgender Equality still lists no X option, so confirm X availability with the DMV before relying on it.
delaware.marker_overview: Delaware allows gender-marker changes on a birth certificate with affidavits from you and a medical or mental health professional, and on a driver's license or state ID with a provider's certification on a DMV form — no court order and no surgery are required. Note: HB 375 (2026), which would have added an X marker and self-attestation, died in House Appropriations, so the existing rules are unchanged.
delaware.surgery_required: No — Delaware does not require surgery; the provider affidavit may cite hormonal, psychological, or other treatment appropriate for the individual for gender transition, and the DMV procedure expressly states surgery is not required.

florida.agency_name: Florida Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics
florida.birth_certificate: Florida is not currently processing gender-marker changes on birth certificates. As reported in July 2024, the state stopped processing these changes, and a September 2026 national review states that Florida does not allow amending the gender marker on a birth certificate at all, with changes continuing to be denied although the state has not publicly provided a new policy. Older guides still describe the former process (forms DH429 and DH430, a physician letter, and a $20 amendment fee), but that route should not be relied on. Contact the Florida Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics, to confirm the current position before submitting anything.
florida.court_order_required: No — a court order does not currently provide a working route to a gender-marker change in Florida, as the state is not processing these changes on birth certificates or licenses; a court order is still the route for a legal name change.
florida.drivers_license: The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles issued a memo on January 26, 2024, rescinding its gender-requirements policy (IR08) and stating that the gender shown on a driver's license or ID card must be taken from a primary identification document. The Department will no longer issue a replacement license to change the gender marker to reflect gender identity, and the memo warned that misrepresenting gender could bring criminal and civil penalties. No X marker is available.
florida.marker_overview: Florida currently restricts gender-marker changes: the state is no longer processing gender-marker changes on birth certificates, and the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles rescinded its driver's license gender-change policy in January 2024. There is no X marker, and there is currently no working process to change the marker on either document.
florida.surgery_required: No — surgery is not the deciding issue in Florida, because the state is not processing gender-marker changes at all, so no surgery or procedure can currently produce a change.

georgia.agency_name: Georgia Department of Public Health, State Office of Vital Records
georgia.birth_certificate: Apply to the Georgia Department of Public Health, State Office of Vital Records, under O.C.G.A. § 31-10-23(e). Submit an Affidavit for Amendment (Form 3977), a certified copy of a court order indicating your sex has been changed by surgical procedure and your name has been changed, a medical certification from the physician's office with the physician's original signature, a copy of valid government-issued photo ID, and payment by money order or cashier's check. The amendment fee is $10 plus the certificate fee.
georgia.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for a birth-certificate change, and for a driver's license a court order is one of the two accepted proofs (the other is a physician's letter).
georgia.drivers_license: Apply at the Georgia Department of Driver Services with either a court order or a physician's letter certifying the gender change, stating your name, date of birth, date of gender reassignment operation, and other identifying information. A passport showing the updated gender can also be used as evidence. Georgia Legal Aid lists a $5 change fee. Some doctors may provide a letter based on treatment other than surgery, such as hormone therapy, but DDS may not accept it. No X marker is offered; only M or F.
georgia.marker_overview: Georgia is restrictive: a birth-certificate change requires a court order stating that sex was changed by surgical procedure and that the person's name was changed. A driver's license or state ID can be changed with a court order or a physician's letter stating the date of a gender reassignment operation. Only M or F markers are available — there is no X option.
georgia.surgery_required: Yes — a birth-certificate change requires a court order stating sex was changed by surgical procedure, and a driver's license change requires a court order or physician's letter stating the date of a gender reassignment operation.

hawaii.agency_name: Hawaii Department of Health, Office of Health Status Monitoring
hawaii.birth_certificate: Apply to the Hawaii Department of Health, Office of Health Status Monitoring, Registration/Corrections Section, with an Application for Amendment to Birth Record and a notarized Physician Affidavit Form for Sex Designation Change. The physician must attest to a bona fide physician-patient relationship, treatment and evaluation, and that the registrant has had appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition and completed the transition. Fee is $3 per amended item. A new certificate is issued and the original is sealed.
hawaii.court_order_required: No — No court order is needed to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is only needed if you are also changing your legal name.
hawaii.drivers_license: Apply through the Hawaii Department of Transportation / county examiner of drivers. Since July 1, 2020, the gender marker on a Hawaii driver's license or state ID can be updated to M, F, or X upon self-attestation by the applicant, with no medical documentation required. A Gender Designation Form is completed at the licensing office.
hawaii.marker_overview: Hawaii allows gender-marker changes on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID. The birth certificate requires a notarized physician affidavit, while a driver's license or state ID can be updated by self-attestation with M, F, or X available since July 1, 2020. No court order is needed for the gender marker itself on either document.
hawaii.surgery_required: No — No surgery is required for either document; the birth certificate requires a physician affidavit of appropriate clinical treatment and completed transition, and the driver's license requires only self-attestation.

idaho.agency_name: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, Bureau of Vital Records and Health Statistics
idaho.birth_certificate: Handled by the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, Bureau of Vital Records and Health Statistics. Sex is a material fact recorded at birth under Idaho Code sections 39-245A and 73-114. Within one year of birth it can be corrected only by a notarized affidavit that the certificate incorrectly recorded a material fact; after one year it can be challenged in court only on fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact. There is no gender-identity amendment path.
idaho.court_order_required: No — A court order does not create a gender-marker change in Idaho; after one year a court proceeding is only available to correct fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact on the record.
idaho.drivers_license: Handled by the Idaho Transportation Department, Division of Motor Vehicles. Idaho licenses and IDs show M or F only, with no X option, and the department no longer publishes a procedure for changing the sex designation. Since 2024 it has required an amended birth certificate or an updated passport for a designation change, so with birth-certificate sex amendments closed, the license marker is effectively unchangeable for most Idaho-born people.
idaho.marker_overview: Idaho currently does not allow gender-marker changes on birth certificates or, in practice, on driver's licenses. A federal injunction that had blocked enforcement since 2018 was dissolved on January 8, 2026, so Idaho now enforces its law requiring birth certificates to reflect the biological sex recorded at birth. Because the transportation department requires an amended birth certificate for a license change, the license marker is effectively unchangeable for most Idaho-born people.
idaho.surgery_required: No — Idaho does not offer a surgery-based route at all; gender-marker changes are not permitted regardless of surgery or medical treatment.

illinois.agency_name: Illinois Department of Public Health, Division of Vital Records
illinois.birth_certificate: Apply by mail to the Illinois Department of Public Health, Division of Vital Records, with a signed and notarized Affidavit and Certificate of Correction Request form, a copy of a non-expired government-issued photo ID, and a $15 fee, which includes one certified copy (additional copies $2 each). No medical signature or documentation is required to change only the gender marker; a certified court order is needed only if also changing the name.
illinois.court_order_required: No — No court order is needed to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license or state ID; a court order is only needed if you are also changing your legal name.
illinois.drivers_license: Visit an Illinois Secretary of State facility in person with a completed Gender Designation Change Form signed by the applicant and a current Illinois driver's license or state ID. M, F, or X is available, with no medical signature or documentation required. Fee is $5 for a driver's license and $10 for a state ID.
illinois.marker_overview: Illinois is one of the most permissive states for gender-marker changes: both the birth certificate and the driver's license or state ID can be updated to M, F, or X by self-attestation, with no court order, medical documentation, or surgery required. Since July 1, 2023, no health care professional certification is needed for a birth certificate, and the X marker has been available on licenses and IDs since January 1, 2024.
illinois.surgery_required: No — No surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; both are changed by the applicant's own signed statement.

indiana.agency_name: Indiana Department of Health, Vital Records
indiana.birth_certificate: On paper, apply to the Indiana Department of Health, Vital Records, with Form 49607 (Application for Search and Certified Copy of Birth Record), a certified copy of a court order for change of gender marker, a photocopy of a valid government-issued ID, and a $10 fee. In practice, the department has not been processing gender-change requests since March 2025 under Executive Order 25-36, and a federal court declined to preliminarily enjoin that policy in September 2025, so confirm current practice before relying on a court order.
indiana.court_order_required: Yes — A court order is required on paper for a birth-certificate gender change, and it was formerly accepted for a driver's license, but the BMV no longer accepts court orders for gender changes as of February 12, 2026, and the Department of Health has not processed birth-certificate gender changes since March 2025.
indiana.drivers_license: Handled by the Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles. Effective February 12, 2026, under amended rule 140 IAC 7-1.1-3, the BMV no longer provides the option to change the gender on an Indiana credential by using a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement. Credentials are issued with M or F only; there is no X option.
indiana.marker_overview: Indiana has sharply restricted gender-marker changes in 2025–2026. On paper, a birth-certificate gender change still requires a court order, but the Indiana Department of Health has not processed gender-change requests since March 2025 under Executive Order 25-36, with litigation ongoing. Effective February 12, 2026, the Bureau of Motor Vehicles no longer changes the gender marker on a driver's license or ID card at all, even with a court order or physician statement.
indiana.surgery_required: No — Indiana law does not require surgery for a birth-certificate change; it requires a court order, and no surgery or medical proof can now change a driver's license marker.

iowa.agency_name: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Health Statistics
iowa.birth_certificate: Handled by the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Health Statistics. As of July 1, 2025, the department is no longer issuing gender-marker amendments on birth certificates under Senate File 418 (Iowa Code sections 4.1A and 144.23). A new birth certificate may now show only the sex observed or clinically verified at birth, and the former process using a notarized physician affidavit of sex-designation treatment was removed.
iowa.court_order_required: No — A court order does not provide a gender-marker change in Iowa; Senate File 418 removed the sex-designation amendment process, so neither a court order nor a physician affidavit can now change an Iowa birth certificate's sex designation.
iowa.drivers_license: Handled by the Iowa Department of Transportation, in person by appointment. Iowa licenses and IDs show M or F only, with no X option. For a person born in Iowa, an amended birth certificate with the updated marker was required, and that route is now closed. People born outside Iowa could previously use an amended out-of-state birth certificate or a notarized physician affidavit, but a DOT rule effective November 19, 2025 (761 IAC 605.4(5)) states the license sex will match the sex on the identity document presented, and whether that leaves any route for out-of-state-born residents is not settled in the official sources reviewed — verify current practice with the DOT before applying.
iowa.marker_overview: Iowa banned gender-marker changes on birth certificates effective July 1, 2025, under Senate File 418, which defines sex as male or female as observed or clinically verified at birth and removed the former physician-affidavit process. Iowa-born people therefore can no longer obtain an amended birth certificate with a new gender marker, which also blocks a license change for them. A driver's license or state ID shows M or F only, with no X option.
iowa.surgery_required: No — Iowa does not require surgery, because gender-marker changes on Iowa birth certificates are no longer permitted at all under Senate File 418, regardless of surgery or treatment.

kansas.agency_name: Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Office of Vital Statistics
kansas.birth_certificate: Handled by the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Office of Vital Statistics. The office no longer processes gender-identity amendments to birth certificates, a policy in place since Senate Bill 180 in 2023. Senate Bill 244 now directs the office to invalidate and reissue birth certificates that were amended due to sex identification so they reflect the individual's sex at birth; a replacement certificate costs $20 per certificate.
kansas.court_order_required: No — A court order does not enable a gender-marker change in Kansas; Senate Bill 244 bars gender-marker changes on both documents and requires previously changed documents to be reverted to sex assigned at birth.
kansas.drivers_license: Handled by the Kansas Department of Revenue, Division of Vehicles. Kansas is no longer amending gender markers on driver's licenses. Under Senate Bill 244, effective February 26, 2026, any driver's license or state ID whose gender marker does not match the sex assigned at birth is invalid, with no grace period; affected residents were directed to surrender the credential and be issued a new one showing the sex assigned at birth, at the standard replacement cost.
kansas.marker_overview: Kansas now bans gender-marker changes on both birth certificates and driver's licenses, and goes further than other states by invalidating documents that were already changed. Senate Bill 244, effective February 26, 2026, requires state documents to list only the sex assigned at birth and directs the state to invalidate and reissue about 1,700 driver's licenses and up to about 1,800 birth certificates that had been amended. There is no X marker and no court-order or medical route around the ban.
kansas.surgery_required: No — Kansas does not offer a surgery-based route; gender-marker changes are banned regardless of surgery or medical treatment.

kentucky.agency_name: Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Office of Vital Statistics
kentucky.birth_certificate: Apply to the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Office of Vital Statistics, under KRS 213.121. The office will amend the certificate upon receipt of a sworn statement by a licensed physician indicating the individual's gender has been changed by surgical procedure, together with a certified copy of a court order changing the individual's name. An amended certificate is marked as amended. A certified copy costs $10.
kentucky.court_order_required: Yes — A court order changing the name is required for the birth-certificate change, and a court order changing the gender marker is one of the accepted proofs for a driver's license (a surgeon's letter or an amended birth certificate also works for the license).
kentucky.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Kentucky Transportation Cabinet Driver Licensing Regional Office. To change the gender marker, present one of: an amended birth certificate showing the correct gender, a court order of gender change, or a letter from the surgeon stating that gender reassignment surgery has been completed. Only M or F is available; there is no X option.
kentucky.marker_overview: Kentucky still allows gender-marker changes, but it is one of the strictest states that does so: a birth-certificate change requires proof of gender reassignment surgery plus a court-ordered name change, and a driver's license change requires an amended birth certificate, a court order changing the gender marker, or a surgeon's letter. Only M or F is available; there is no X option on either document.
kentucky.surgery_required: Yes — Kentucky requires proof of gender reassignment surgery for a birth-certificate change, and a surgeon's letter confirming completed surgery is one accepted proof for a driver's license (a court order or an amended birth certificate is an alternative for the license).

louisiana.agency_name: Louisiana Department of Health, Vital Records Registry (Center for Vital Records and Statistics)
louisiana.birth_certificate: Apply to the Louisiana Department of Health, Vital Records Registry, under La. R.S. 40:62. First obtain a court order certifying the gender change; the court must be convinced the petitioner was properly diagnosed, that sex reassignment or corrective surgery was properly performed, and that the anatomical structure of the petitioner's sex has changed. Then submit a certified copy of the court order, an Application to Amend Birth Certificate, a copy of the original birth certificate, and a copy of a photo ID. The amendment fee is $27.50, which includes one certified copy of the new record.
louisiana.court_order_required: Yes — A court order certifying the gender change is required for a birth certificate; for a driver's license a court judgment is one accepted proof, but a physician's statement of a successful change is also accepted.
louisiana.drivers_license: Apply at a Louisiana Office of Motor Vehicles field office. To change the gender marker, present a medical statement signed by a physician stating the applicant has undergone a successful gender change or reassignment, a corrected birth certificate showing the change, or a court judgment specifying the change of sex. Licenses show M or F; no X option is listed in the sources reviewed.
louisiana.marker_overview: Louisiana still allows gender-marker changes, but only through a court process that requires proof of surgery for a birth certificate. A birth certificate is changed only on a court order certifying the gender change, while a driver's license can be changed with a physician's statement of a successful gender change, a corrected birth certificate, or a court judgment. Only M or F is available; no X option is listed in the sources reviewed.
louisiana.surgery_required: Yes — A court order for a birth-certificate change requires proof that sex reassignment or corrective surgery was properly performed; a driver's license change requires a physician's statement of a successful gender change or reassignment.

maine.agency_name: Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Maine CDC, Data, Research, and Vital Statistics
maine.birth_certificate: Apply to the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Maine CDC, Data, Research, and Vital Statistics. An adult 18 or older completes the Application to Correct a Vital Record (Form VS-7), has it notarized, and mails it with a $60 fee; no physician's letter or court order is needed, and M, F, or X may be selected. For a minor, a parent or legal guardian applies and must also submit a health care professional declaration affirming the requested gender aligns with the minor's gender identity.
maine.court_order_required: No — No court order is needed to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license or state ID; a court order is only needed for a separate legal name change, unless a first or middle name change is made at the same time as the birth-certificate gender change.
maine.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Maine Bureau of Motor Vehicles location with a new license or Real ID application and a Gender Designation Form; a new photo is taken. M, F, or X may be selected, with no medical provider certification required. The X option has been available on Maine licenses and IDs since 2018, and the Secretary of State confirmed in March 2025 that it remains available.
maine.marker_overview: Maine is one of the most permissive states: adults can change the gender marker on a birth certificate with a simple notarized application and on a driver's license or state ID with a gender designation form, with M, F, or X available on both and no court order, doctor's letter, or surgery required for adults. The Secretary of State reaffirmed on March 3, 2025, that the X option and gender-marker changes on licenses remain available despite the 2025 federal executive order on sex designations.
maine.surgery_required: No — No surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for an adult to change the gender marker on either document; for a minor's birth certificate, a health care professional declaration is required, but not surgery.

maryland.agency_name: Maryland Department of Health, Vital Statistics Administration
maryland.birth_certificate: Apply to the Maryland Department of Health, Vital Statistics Administration, with the application for change in sex designation, a government-issued photo ID, and a $10 fee for the new certificate plus $10 for a copy. Proof is a signed statement from a licensed health care practitioner who treated or evaluated the applicant, stating the applicant has undergone surgical, hormonal, or other treatment appropriate for sex transition or has an intersex condition, or a court order indicating the sex has been changed. A court order is also needed if changing the name at the same time. Under Senate Bill 314 (effective October 1, 2025), the practitioner letter is replaced by the applicant's own statement under penalty of perjury and X is expressly allowed — confirm the current form before filing.
maryland.court_order_required: No — No court order is required for either document; a court order is an optional alternative proof for a birth certificate, and a separate judicial declaration of gender identity is available but not required.
maryland.drivers_license: Apply at the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, by appointment. Under Md. Code, Transportation section 12-305, an applicant may indicate female, male, or unspecified/other, which displays as X on the license, ID card, or moped permit. The MVA may not require proof of the applicant's sex and may not deny the application because the selected sex does not match another document. No documentation is needed unless also changing the name.
maryland.marker_overview: Maryland allows gender-marker changes on both documents, with the driver's license handled entirely by self-attestation and the birth certificate by a health care practitioner's statement or a court order. M, F, or X is available on both. Maryland law changed in 2025: Senate Bill 314, the Birth Certificate Modernization Act, effective October 1, 2025, modernized the birth-certificate process, replacing the medical-provider letter with the applicant's own statement under penalty of perjury and clarifying that X is allowed — confirm the current application form with the Vital Statistics Administration, as the statute text retrieved still lists the practitioner-statement route.
maryland.surgery_required: No — No surgery or medical procedure is required; a birth certificate needs a health care practitioner's statement of appropriate treatment (surgical, hormonal, or other) or a court order, and a driver's license needs no documentation at all.

massachusetts.agency_name: Registry of Vital Records and Statistics, Massachusetts Department of Public Health
massachusetts.birth_certificate: Apply to the Registry of Vital Records and Statistics (Massachusetts Department of Public Health), or to the clerk of the city or town where the birth occurred, with the Applicant Affidavit in Support of Amendment of a Birth Certificate for Sex (form R116), signed under penalty of perjury; if mailed, the affidavit must be notarized. No medical documentation, court order, or proof of a name change is required for the marker change; a certified copy of a legal name-change decree is only needed if you are also changing your name. Fee: $50 one-time amendment fee, plus $32 per certified copy by mail ($20 in person).
massachusetts.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name.
massachusetts.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) Service Center with a new License/ID Card Application indicating the correct gender marker (M, F, or X). No documentation is required for the gender designation under M.G.L. c. 90, § 8N, and the X marker has been available on licenses and state IDs since November 2019. A name change requires first updating Social Security and bringing a certified copy of the court-ordered name change.
massachusetts.marker_overview: Massachusetts lets you change the gender marker on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with M, F, or X available on both documents. No court order, doctor's letter, or surgery is required for the marker itself; a court order is only needed if you are also changing your legal name. A July 2024 law (M.G.L. c. 46, § 13(e) and c. 90, § 8N) streamlined the birth-certificate process and added the X option to birth records.
massachusetts.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; the statute expressly bars officials from requiring any medical or health-care documentation for a marker change.

michigan.agency_name: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS), Vital Records
michigan.birth_certificate: Mail the Application to Correct or Change a Michigan Birth Record and the State of Michigan Sex Designation Form, plus a photocopy of a photo ID, to MDHHS Vital Records. No medical documentation, physician's signature, court order, or surgery is required for the marker change. Fee: $50, which includes one certified copy of the amended certificate; extra copies are $16 each, and optional rush processing (2–3 weeks instead of about 6 weeks) costs an extra $25.
michigan.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name.
michigan.drivers_license: Complete the Michigan Secretary of State Sex Designation Form and bring it with your current license or ID to a Secretary of State office in person; you select M, F, or X by self-attestation. No medical documentation, court order, or birth-certificate change is required. Fee: $9 to correct a driver's license, $10 for a state ID; a new photo is taken and the new card is mailed within about two to three weeks.
michigan.marker_overview: Michigan lets you change the gender marker on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with M, F, or X available on both documents. No court order, medical documentation, or surgery is required for the marker itself; a court order is only needed if you are also changing your legal name. The birth-certificate change is an administrative amendment through the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS), and the license change is done in person at a Secretary of State office.
michigan.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical treatment, or doctor's letter is required for either document; both the birth-certificate and license forms are self-attestation only.

minnesota.agency_name: Minnesota Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
minnesota.birth_certificate: Submit a Birth Record Amendment Request to the MDH Office of Vital Records, indicating 'sex' as the item to amend, with either an original letter from a licensed physician certifying appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or a certified copy of a court order specifically directing amendment of the sex on the birth record. The request must be signed in front of a notary. Fee: $40 amendment fee plus $26 for a certificate with the amended information. Note: if the change is made by amendment without a court order, later certificates note that data items were amended; a court order directing MDH to replace the record seals the original instead. MDH does not publish an X option for birth records.
minnesota.court_order_required: Yes — for a birth certificate only, and only if you do not provide a physician's letter certifying appropriate clinical treatment; a driver's license or state ID never requires a court order.
minnesota.drivers_license: Minnesota Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) lets you choose M, F, or X on a driver's license or state ID by self-designation — it works like changing the eye-color field, with no medical documentation, court order, or extra form required. Just indicate your preferred marker when you apply for or renew your license or ID.
minnesota.marker_overview: Minnesota splits the rules by document: a driver's license or state ID can be changed to M, F, or X by self-designation with no medical documentation or court order, but a birth certificate requires either a physician's letter certifying appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or a court order directing the change. The birth-certificate change goes through the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) Office of Vital Records. A 2026 bill (S.F. 5300) that would allow birth-record marker changes by sworn statement has only been introduced, not passed.
minnesota.surgery_required: No — no surgery or medical procedure is required for either document; the birth-certificate physician's letter certifies appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, which is not a surgery requirement, and no medical proof of any kind is needed for a driver's license.

mississippi.agency_name: Mississippi State Department of Health, Office of Vital Records
mississippi.birth_certificate: Apply to the Mississippi State Department of Health, Office of Vital Records, with Form 1126 (Affidavit to Amend Mississippi Birth Certificate), a certified copy of a court order for change of gender marker, and a physician's letter (medical statement attesting to the reassignment). The change is recorded only as a marginal notation on the original certificate — no new certificate is issued — and only M and F markers are available. Fee: $28, which includes one certified copy; additional copies are $6 each.
mississippi.court_order_required: Yes — a certified court order (plus a medical statement) is required for the birth-certificate marginal notation; for a driver's license, even a court order cannot change the marker after July 1, 2026.
mississippi.drivers_license: As of July 1, 2026, the Mississippi Department of Public Safety must issue every new, renewal, or duplicate driver's license, temporary permit, or commercial license with a sex designation consistent with the sex determined at birth (SB 2322, Miss. Code Ann. § 63-1-35(7)). The designation cannot be changed to reflect gender identity, and a court order inconsistent with this rule has no effect on license issuance or renewal. The only permitted changes are corrections of a scrivener's error, a sex misidentified at birth due to a verifiable disorder of sex development, or a license previously altered to record a sex other than the sex at birth. No X marker is available.
mississippi.marker_overview: Mississippi is now one of the most restrictive states for gender marker changes. Since July 1, 2026, under SB 2322 (Miss. Code Ann. § 63-1-35(7)), every new, renewal, or duplicate driver's license or state ID must show the sex determined at birth, and a court order cannot override that — only a scrivener's error, a verifiable disorder of sex development, or a correction of a license previously altered away from the birth sex can change it. A birth certificate can still record a sex change, but only as a marginal notation (no new certificate is issued), and only with a certified court order plus a medical statement attesting to the reassignment. There is no X option on any Mississippi document.
mississippi.surgery_required: Yes — for a birth certificate, the state requires a physician's letter (medical statement attesting to the reassignment) in addition to a court order; for a driver's license, the marker cannot be changed to reflect gender identity at all after July 1, 2026, regardless of medical evidence.

missouri.agency_name: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Bureau of Vital Records
missouri.birth_certificate: Obtain a certified copy of a court order from a court of competent jurisdiction indicating that the sex of the person born in Missouri has been changed by surgical procedure and that the person's name has been changed (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 193.215(9)), then mail it with a signed cover letter requesting the order be applied to the record to the Bureau of Vital Records, Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, in Jefferson City. Fee: $15 processing fee, plus $15 per certified copy of the amended certificate.
missouri.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for a birth certificate, and for a driver's license it is one of the two accepted routes (the other being proof of gender-affirming surgery).
missouri.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Missouri Department of Revenue license office with either a certified court order declaring the new gender designation or a signed letter from a surgeon confirming gender-affirming surgery. This replaced the pre-August 2024 process, under which a form signed by a physician, therapist, or social worker was enough. Only M and F markers are offered; there is no X option, and the change cannot be done online or by mail.
missouri.marker_overview: Missouri is restrictive and became more so in August 2024, when the Department of Revenue ended its physician-form process for driver's licenses. A birth-certificate change requires a court order stating the sex was changed by surgical procedure (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 193.215(9)), and a driver's license change now requires either a court order or proof of gender-affirming surgery. There is no X marker option, and no standard court form exists for a gender-marker petition, so the court step usually requires a custom petition.
missouri.surgery_required: Yes — the birth-certificate statute requires a court order stating the sex was changed by surgical procedure, and a driver's license change requires either such a court order or documented proof of gender-affirming surgery.

montana.agency_name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Office of Vital Records
montana.birth_certificate: While the injunction is in effect, apply to the DPHHS Office of Vital Records under the restored 2017 rule with an Affidavit for Correction of a Vital Record and the department's Gender Designation Form (your own certification of gender transition or an intersex condition), or with a government-issued ID showing the correct gender, or a certified court order. No court order, medical documentation, or surgery is required while the injunction stands. Fee: $41, which includes one certified copy; additional copies are $16 each. Caution: the underlying ban (SB 280, the 2022 DPHHS rule, and SB 458) remains on the books and could take effect again if the injunction is lifted, since the case is still pending on the merits.
montana.court_order_required: No — no court order is required for a birth certificate while the injunction is in effect; for a driver's license, a court order is one accepted route, but an amended birth certificate works instead.
montana.drivers_license: Apply in person at a Montana Motor Vehicle Division (MVD) office with an amended birth certificate showing your preferred gender or a certified copy of a court order for change of gender, plus proof of identity, your current license or ID, and updated Social Security information. The MVD policy that blocked these changes is also covered by the preliminary injunction affirmed in April 2026. Only M and F markers are available; Montana offers no X option on driver's licenses or state IDs.
montana.marker_overview: Montana's gender-marker rules are currently set by litigation, not by the text printed in the code. The state enacted a 2021 law (SB 280) requiring surgery plus a court order for birth-certificate changes, then a 2022 Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) rule banning such changes outright, and a Motor Vehicle Division (MVD) policy blocking license changes — but a preliminary injunction against all of those policies was affirmed by the Montana Supreme Court on April 14, 2026 (Kalarchik v. State, 2026 MT 76), so while the injunction is in effect, birth certificates can be changed by affidavit with no surgery or court order, and licenses can be changed with an amended birth certificate or court order. Only M and F markers are issued; X availability is still in litigation.
montana.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required while the injunction is in effect; note, however, that the state's blocked 2021 law (SB 280) would require surgery plus a court order if the injunction were lifted.

nebraska.agency_name: Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, Vital Records
nebraska.birth_certificate: Submit an Application for Amendment to the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, Vital Records, with a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery (stating the surgery and its date) and a certified copy of a court order changing the person's name, as required by Neb. Rev. Stat. § 71-604.01. A new birth certificate is issued and the original is sealed. Fee: $16 amendment fee plus $17 per certified copy.
nebraska.court_order_required: Yes — a court order changing the name is required as part of a birth-certificate change (alongside the surgeon's affidavit); no court order is needed for a driver's license, which uses the provider-signed certification form instead.
nebraska.drivers_license: Apply in person at any Nebraska Department of Motor Vehicles driver licensing office (this cannot be done online) with acceptable proof of identification, a completed Certification of Sex Reassignment form signed by a Doctor of Medicine, Doctor of Osteopathy, Physician Assistant, Advanced Practice Nurse, or Doctor of Chiropractic certifying that you have undergone the procedures required for social gender recognition, plus a completed license data form and two proofs of address if your address is unverified. Only F or M markers are available; Nebraska offers no X option on driver's licenses or state IDs.
nebraska.marker_overview: Nebraska is restrictive: a birth-certificate change requires both a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery and a court order changing the person's name (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 71-604.01). A driver's license change is somewhat easier — it needs a Certification of Sex Reassignment form signed by a medical provider certifying procedures required for social gender recognition, with no proof of surgery demanded by the DMV form itself — but there is no X option on any Nebraska document, and a 2023 governor's executive order defines gender by reproductive function for state documents.
nebraska.surgery_required: Yes — a birth-certificate change requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery; a driver's license requires a medical provider's certification of procedures required for social gender recognition, though the DMV form itself does not demand proof of surgery.

nevada.agency_name: Nevada Division of Public and Behavioral Health, Office of Vital Records and Statistics
nevada.birth_certificate: Mail an Application for a Correction of Birth Record, a notarized Affidavit for Correction of a Record, and a Supplemental Affidavit completed by someone with personal knowledge that you identify as the requested gender (or, instead of the Supplemental Affidavit, a written statement on letterhead from a licensed health-care professional or a court order confirming the change) to the Nevada Office of Vital Records and Statistics, with a copy of the original birth certificate if available. A certified court order is only needed if you are also changing your name. Fee: $40, which includes one certified copy of the amended certificate; additional copies are $20 each.
nevada.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name.
nevada.drivers_license: At a Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles office, simply indicate your preferred gender designation (M, F, or X) on the application for a new license or ID. No medical documentation or certification is needed, and Nevada does not require the gender on your license to match the gender on your other documents. A name change requires a certified court order and an updated Social Security record first.
nevada.marker_overview: Nevada makes gender marker changes relatively simple on both documents, with M, F, or X available on each. A birth certificate is changed with notarized affidavits — no court order, medical documentation, or surgery is required — and a driver's license marker is changed by simply selecting your preferred designation on the application, with no medical certification at all. A name change is a separate court process, but the gender marker can be changed on its own.
nevada.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; the birth-certificate Supplemental Affidavit can be completed by any person who knows you, not a medical professional.

new-hampshire.agency_name: New Hampshire Secretary of State, Division of Vital Records Administration
new-hampshire.birth_certificate: Apply to the clerk of the city or town where the birth occurred with Form VSCr (Application for Correcting or Completing a Certificate of Birth), a certified copy of a court order advising that the person has had a sex change (RSA 5-C:87(V)), and a photocopy of a valid photo ID; the clerk then prepares a new birth record reflecting the change. The court order does not require proof of surgery, but what a court will order can vary by judge, and X is not recognized on birth certificates. Fee: $10 amendment fee plus $15 per certified copy.
new-hampshire.court_order_required: Yes — a court order is required for a birth-certificate change only; no court order is needed for a driver's license or state ID.
new-hampshire.drivers_license: At a New Hampshire Division of Motor Vehicles office, choose F, M, or X on the license or ID application (form DSMV 450 for a gender-marker update). No medical documentation, provider certification, or court order is required — the health-care provider certification requirement was removed in August 2021, and the X option has been available since January 1, 2020 under HB 669. The fee for the marker change is $3. Minors can also select X with parental consent.
new-hampshire.marker_overview: New Hampshire splits the rules by document: a driver's license or state ID can be changed to F, M, or X by self-identification with no medical documentation or court order, but a birth certificate requires a court order for a 'sex change' under RSA 5-C:87, and X is not recognized on birth certificates. The license rules have survived recent repeal attempts — 2026 bills to remove the X marker (HB 1165) and to strip gender identity from nondiscrimination law (HB 1564) did not become law.
new-hampshire.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; the birth-certificate court order does not require proof of surgery, and the license change is by self-identification alone.

new-jersey.agency_name: New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Vital Statistics and Registry
new-jersey.birth_certificate: Submit the Request Form and Attestation to Amend Sex Designation on a Birth Certificate (REG-L2 for adults, REG-L3 for a minor's parent or guardian) to the New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Vital Statistics and Registry, Records Modification Unit, by mail or through the office's online system, selecting Female, Male, or Undesignated/Non-binary and attesting under penalty of perjury that the change conforms your legal gender to your gender identity and is not for a fraudulent purpose. Include a copy of your birth certificate or current government ID; a certified copy of a name-change court order is only needed if you are also changing your name. Fee: $2 to process the change, plus $25 for the first certified copy of the amended certificate and $2 for each additional copy. The amended certificate is not marked as amended and the original is placed under seal.
new-jersey.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name, and New Jersey courts can issue a gender-declaration order for residents born in states that do require one.
new-jersey.drivers_license: Complete the Declaration of Gender Designation Change form and bring it in person to any New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) Licensing Center, surrendering your current license or ID. You may indicate M, F, or X (non-binary/unspecified) by self-attestation — no medical documentation or doctor's signature is needed. Fee: $11 for the duplicate card.
new-jersey.marker_overview: New Jersey lets you change the gender marker on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with Female, Male, or Undesignated/Non-binary (X on licenses) available on both. No medical documentation, doctor's signature, or surgery is required for either document, under the 2018 Babs Siperstein Law (N.J.S.A. 26:8-40.12, effective February 1, 2019), which ended the old surgery-proof requirement. A court order is needed only if you are also changing your legal name.
new-jersey.surgery_required: No — no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter is required for either document; the 2018 Babs Siperstein Law expressly removed the prior requirement of proof of gender reassignment surgery.

new-mexico.agency_name: New Mexico Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Records
new-mexico.birth_certificate: Apply to the New Mexico Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Records, using the Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form (adult, parent/guardian, or two-parent versions; minors age 14 and older must also sign a consent form). The form is a statement signed under penalty of perjury and must be signed before a notary. A certified court order is needed only if the legal name is also being changed. The fee is $20, which includes one new birth certificate, with additional copies $10 each. The certificate is reissued showing male, female, or X and is not marked amended. Note: once an item on a vital record has been amended, it cannot be amended again without a certified court order.
new-mexico.court_order_required: No — no court order is needed to change the gender marker on either a birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is required only if the legal name is also being changed, or to amend the same birth-record item a second time.
new-mexico.drivers_license: Apply to the New Mexico Motor Vehicle Division using Form MVD-10237 (Request for Sex Designation Change), a sworn statement signed under penalty of perjury and notarized, choosing male, female, or X. No medical documentation and no court order are required for the marker change; a court order is needed only if the name is also being changed. A standard replacement-card fee applies.
new-mexico.marker_overview: New Mexico allows a gender marker change on both a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with male, female, and X options on both documents. No court order, doctor's letter, or surgery is required for the marker change itself. The process comes from Senate Bill 20 (2019), which amended state law to allow reissue of a birth certificate based on a sworn statement of gender identity.
new-mexico.surgery_required: No — New Mexico requires no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter for a gender marker change on either document; a sworn statement of gender identity is all that is needed.

new-york.agency_name: New York State Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Records
new-york.birth_certificate: Apply to the New York State Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Records, which handles births outside New York City (New York City births go through the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene). Adults file the Application for Amendment of Certificate of Birth for Gender Designation for an Adult (DOH-5305) plus a notarized Affidavit of Gender Error (DOH-5303); minors use forms DOH-5306 and DOH-5304, signed by a parent or legal guardian. One certified copy of the amended certificate is provided free, and additional copies are $30 each. A court order is needed only if the name is also being changed.
new-york.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on a New York birth certificate or driver's license; the Gender Recognition Act states that no court order is required to amend a state-issued identity document, and a court order is needed only for a legal name change.
new-york.drivers_license: Apply to the New York State Department of Motor Vehicles by completing the Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44) at a DMV office, or through the DMV's online transaction, and choosing M, F, or X. No medical documentation or court order is required. A standard replacement fee applies.
new-york.marker_overview: New York allows a gender marker change on a birth certificate and a driver's license or state ID by self-attestation, with male, female, and X options on both documents. No court order, doctor's letter, or surgery is required. The rules come from the Gender Recognition Act, which took effect in late 2021, with the DMV X option added in June 2022.
new-york.surgery_required: No — New York requires no surgery, medical procedure, or doctor's letter for a gender marker change on either document; the change is made by self-attestation.

north-carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Public Health, Vital Records
north-carolina.birth_certificate: Apply to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Public Health, Vital Records, using the Birth Certificate Modifications Form, with a $39 fee. Submit a sworn statement plus proof of gender identity, such as a government-issued ID or passport already showing the requested marker, or a certification of gender identity signed by a licensed health care professional, social worker, or case manager. Although the text of N.C. Gen. Stat. section 130A-118 still refers to sex reassignment surgery, a 2022 federal consent decree (Kadel v. Folwell) requires Vital Records to amend the marker on proof of gender identity instead, with no surgery required. Note a December 2025 change: for sex changes processed on or after December 1, 2025, state law requires the amended certificate to be attached to the original certificate as a multi-page document, so certified copies now include both pages and the original is no longer sealed and replaced. A court order is needed only if the legal name is also being changed.
north-carolina.court_order_required: No — no court order is required to change the gender marker on a North Carolina driver's license or birth certificate; a court order is needed only for a legal name change.
north-carolina.drivers_license: Apply to the North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles with Form DL-300 (Sex Designation Form), signed by the applicant and by a licensed professional — a physician, psychiatrist, physician's assistant, licensed therapist, counselor, psychologist, case worker, or social worker — certifying the applicant's gender identity. A U.S. passport, a birth certificate, or a U.S. court order showing the requested marker is also accepted instead of the form. Surrender the old license, have a new photo taken, and pay the license fee. Only male or female markers are issued; there is no X option, and no surgery or medical procedure is required.
north-carolina.marker_overview: North Carolina allows a gender marker change on both a birth certificate and a driver's license, but only as male or female — there is no X option on either document. No court order is required for the marker itself, but a licensed professional must certify the person's gender identity for the driver's license, and proof of gender identity is required for the birth certificate. Policy changed in 2022, when a federal consent decree ended the old surgery requirement for birth certificates, and again in December 2025, when a new state law changed how amended certificates are issued (see birth certificate below).
north-carolina.surgery_required: No — North Carolina does not require surgery or any medical procedure to change the gender marker on either document; the driver's license needs a licensed professional's certification of gender identity, and the birth certificate needs proof of gender identity, but neither requires surgery (the surgery language still in the birth-certificate statute was overridden by the 2022 federal consent decree).

north-dakota.agency_name: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Vital Records
north-dakota.birth_certificate: Birth records are handled by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Vital Records. Under N.D.C.C. section 23-02.1-25.1, the sex designation on a birth record may not be amended due to a gender identity change. It may be amended or corrected only if the sex was listed incorrectly because of a scrivener's or data-entry error, the sex was misidentified at birth and the request includes genetic testing results identifying the person's sex, or the person's sex was changed with anatomically correct genitalia for the new sex, certified by a medical provider. In practice, a gender-identity-based marker change on a North Dakota birth certificate is barred.
north-dakota.court_order_required: No — a court order is not the route in North Dakota and does not create a path to change a birth-certificate marker for gender identity; the driver's license change requires a health care provider's certification, not a court order.
north-dakota.drivers_license: Apply to the North Dakota Department of Transportation, Driver License Division, using Form SFN 61146 (Gender Designation Form, revised April 2026). A health care provider — physician, physician assistant, advanced practice nurse, psychologist, or psychiatrist — must certify that a gender role transition has been completed and is permanent. Only male and female markers are available; there is no X option on North Dakota licenses or IDs.
north-dakota.marker_overview: North Dakota restricts gender marker changes. Since House Bill 1297 took effect in 2023 (N.D.C.C. section 23-02.1-25.1), the sex designation on a North Dakota birth record may not be amended because of a gender identity change, with only narrow exceptions. A driver's license or state ID marker can still be changed to male or female only — there is no X option — with a health care provider's certification of a completed, permanent gender role transition.
north-dakota.surgery_required: Yes — for a birth certificate, the only gender-related route is a sex change with anatomically correct genitalia for the new sex, certified by a medical provider; a driver's license instead requires a health care provider's certification of a completed, permanent gender role transition, not proof of a specific surgery.

ohio.agency_name: Ohio Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics
ohio.birth_certificate: Birth records are handled by the Ohio Department of Health, Bureau of Vital Statistics, but a sex-marker correction is pursued through the probate court in the county where the person lives, under Ohio Revised Code section 3705.15. In 2020 a federal court struck down Ohio's old ban on correcting birth-certificate gender markers, and the Department of Health set up a correction process. However, in November 2024 the Ohio Supreme Court could not reach a majority in In re Application for Correction of Birth Record of Adelaide, so there is no controlling precedent and probate courts interpret the statute differently — check with the local probate court before filing. No fee for this process was verified in an official source I could confirm.
ohio.court_order_required: Yes — changing the sex marker on an Ohio birth certificate goes through a county probate court order, and since August 2026 the driver's license marker effectively depends on first obtaining a corrected birth certificate (or passport) showing the desired marker.
ohio.drivers_license: The Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles no longer accepts the Declaration of Gender Change form (BMV 2369) that a physician, psychologist, or therapist used to sign. The BMV now requires an updated birth certificate or a U.S. passport showing the desired marker, and says it will record the sex stated on that document on the Ohio driver's license or ID card. Only male and female markers are issued; there is no X option. Name changes on a license still work as before, with a certified court order.
ohio.marker_overview: Ohio restricts gender marker changes, and the rules changed in August 2026. Around August 18, 2026, the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles stopped accepting its Declaration of Gender Change form (BMV 2369), which had been the way to change a license marker with a provider's statement, citing Ohio Revised Code section 9.05 (added by the 2025 state budget bill), which states the state recognizes only two sexes, male and female, as assigned at birth. The BMV now says it will record the sex shown on the person's birth certificate or passport. Changing an Ohio birth certificate requires a county probate court proceeding, and since a 2024 Ohio Supreme Court case ended without a majority, courts in different counties do not all handle these requests the same way.
ohio.surgery_required: No — Ohio does not state a surgery requirement for a birth-certificate correction or a license marker; the barrier since August 2026 is the BMV's refusal of the provider form and the county-by-county court process for the birth certificate.

oklahoma.agency_name: Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records
oklahoma.birth_certificate: Birth records are handled by the Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records, which processes amendments generally (a $15 application fee and a $25 amendment fee apply to other kinds of corrections). However, the sex designation on an Oklahoma birth certificate may not be amended to reflect gender identity: state law requires it to be male or female as identified at birth, and the Oklahoma Supreme Court confirmed in Fowler v. Stitt (2026) that it cannot be changed even where the person holds a court order. There is currently no path to change the gender marker on an Oklahoma birth certificate.
oklahoma.court_order_required: No — a court order does not create a path in Oklahoma; the Oklahoma Supreme Court confirmed in 2026 that the birth-certificate sex designation cannot be changed even with a court order, and the driver's license rules that once allowed changes were repealed in March 2026.
oklahoma.drivers_license: Driver's licenses and state IDs are issued by Service Oklahoma. The administrative rules that once allowed a replacement license after a sex change were repealed by House Joint Resolution 1032, signed March 3, 2026, so Service Oklahoma no longer processes new gender marker changes on driver's licenses or state IDs. Only male and female markers are issued, and there is no X option. A legal name can still be updated on a license with a certified court order.
oklahoma.marker_overview: Oklahoma bans gender marker changes on both state documents — this is one of the most restrictive states in this set. Executive Order 2021-24 directed the Health Department to stop amending sex designations on birth certificates, Senate Bill 1100 (2022) limited birth-certificate sex designations to male or female only, and House Bill 1225 (2026) reaffirmed that the designation must be the biological sex identified at birth. In March 2026, House Joint Resolution 1032 repealed the Service Oklahoma rules that had allowed driver's license marker changes. In September 2026 the Oklahoma Supreme Court confirmed in Fowler v. Stitt that the birth-certificate sex designation cannot be changed even with a court order. No X marker is available on any Oklahoma document. Legal name changes are still possible with a court order.
oklahoma.surgery_required: No — Oklahoma does not offer a surgery-based route; marker changes are barred outright on both documents, so surgery or any other medical proof does not make a change possible.

oregon.agency_name: Oregon Health Authority, Center for Health Statistics (Oregon Vital Records)
oregon.birth_certificate: Apply to the Oregon Health Authority, Center for Health Statistics (Oregon Vital Records), using Form OHA 2673, the Application to Change the Name and/or Sex on a Record of Live Birth to Support Gender Identity. Sign the form before a notary, include a copy of a valid government-issued photo ID, and pay the $35 amendment fee plus a $25 to $30 certificate fee depending on birth year. A certified copy of a court order for change of gender is also accepted instead of the notarized application. The administrative route can be used only once for the name and once for the sex; any later change requires a court order.
oregon.court_order_required: No — no court order is required for a first gender marker change on either an Oregon birth certificate or a driver's license; a court order is an optional alternative for the birth certificate and is required only for a second change to the same record.
oregon.drivers_license: Visit an Oregon DMV office in person with the current license, permit, or ID card and choose M (male), F (female), or X (not specified) as the gender marker.
